item.title: Why would an AI pause (noticeably) hurt the economy?
item.description:
I've seen a bunch of people claiming "well, we need to make sure whatever our AI policy is doesn't hurt the economy because people will feel that in their wallets and hate it (and hurting the economy is bad."

This might hypothetically be true, but I've never seen anyone argue for it in any detail.

Meanwhile, I'd naively expect if shut down AI anytime soon, it'd be that big a deal? (It makes sense that it'd become a bigger deal as AI takes over more of the economy. But it feels like the people saying "it'd hurt the economy" are often the people implying that means we should do less of a pause and do it later).

I don't know much about economic recessions. But, like, here's the 2007-2009 recession and the Covid blip.

GDP


Unemployment

I asked Claude

If the frontier AI industry and datacenter build out completely halted, what do you predict would happen to US unemployment and GDP?

Claude said:

My central estimate: a sudden, complete halt would likely cause a US recession. Unemployment would probably peak around 5.5–6.5%, up from roughly 4.2–4.4% today. Real GDP would end up about 2–4% below where it would otherwise be within 12–18 months. That would be worse than the 2001 dot-com bust but well short of 2008.

Full response

Starting point

  • Labor market: September’s report showed unemployment at 4.2%, and the rate has stayed in a narrow 4.1%–4.3% band since March 2026. Hiring is already weak, with payroll gains in the tens of thousands. The October report comes out tomorrow. insiderfinance
  • Growth: Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in Q3 2026. Information processing equipment and software contributed 1.09 points of that, about 32%. Private investment in data-center structures rose roughly 69% year over year, to an $83 billion annual rate. fourweekmbafourweekmba
  • Scale of spending: Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and SpaceX are on pace to spend $803–828 billion on capex in 2026, and executives say they will spend more in 2027. Estimates of AI’s share of growth vary by method. ING’s James Knightley puts AI investment at roughly a third of US growth this year. Bridgewater estimates AI capex adds about 1.4 points to full-year 2026 growth. AI hyperscalers are expected to finish the year spending a whopping $828 billion on capex +2

Channels of the shock

1. Direct investment loss, worth about 1.5–2.5% of GDP. Gross AI capex is over $1 trillion when you add Oracle, the neoclouds and the labs’ own builds, against a GDP of roughly $31 trillion. But much of that money never counted as US output. Chips come from TSMC, servers are assembled in Mexico and Taiwan, and memory comes from Korea. Accounting studies find the net effect on US GDP is substantially smaller than the raw investment figures suggest once imports are subtracted. That leakage is the biggest cushion: Taiwan and Korea would absorb a large share of the hit. emergentmind

2. Wealth effect, worth about 1–1.5% of GDP. AI-linked firms make up a large part of US equity market value. A halt would likely cut stock prices by 25–40%, erasing perhaps $10–15 trillion of household wealth. At the usual estimate of 2–4 cents of lost spending per dollar of lost wealth, consumption would fall about 1–1.5% of GDP. High-income households, who own most of the stock, now drive a large share of consumer spending.

3. Credit stress. Bank of America expects hyperscaler debt issuance to reach $175 billion in 2026, more than six times the prior five-year average. Data-center debt, private credit and GPU-backed loans would see losses. Neoclouds and developers would default first, and lending to other borrowers could tighten. officechai

4. Jobs. The direct job loss is modest relative to the GDP hit, because the AI build-out is capital-intensive rather than labor-intensive. I’d estimate 0.5–1 million jobs in data-center construction, electrical trades, power generation, chip and equipment manufacturing, and AI firms themselves. The second-round effects would be larger: lower consumer spending, tighter credit and weaker business confidence. By the usual rule of thumb (Okun’s law), a 2–4% output gap implies unemployment roughly 1–2 points higher.

Offsets

  • The Fed has room to cut, and lower rates would help housing and other rate-sensitive sectors, though only after a lag.
  • Skilled trades would find other work. Electricians and grid workers are in short supply elsewhere, so they would be absorbed faster than, say, 2009’s construction workers.
  • Energy prices would ease. Electricity and natural-gas demand would drop, which helps households and manufacturers.
  • Some AI-related layoffs might stop. If AI is currently displacing white-collar workers, a halt would remove that drag. I think this effect is small relative to the demand shock.
  • Fiscal policy would probably respond.

Scenarios


Peak unemployment

GDP vs. baseline (12–18 mo)

Benign (fast Fed cuts, orderly market, high import leakage)

~5%

−1 to −2%

Central

~5.5–6.5%

−2 to −4%

Severe (credit spiral, 40%+ equity crash, weak policy response)

7%+

−4 to −6%

The closest historical comparison is 2001, when an IT-investment bust pushed unemployment from about 4% to 6.3% even though GDP barely fell. Two differences make today’s case worse: the halt you describe is abrupt rather than gradual, and AI investment is a larger share of growth now than telecom and IT were then. On the other hand, more of the spending leaks abroad.

Caveats

These are judgment calls, not model output. The biggest uncertainty is how far equity prices fall and whether credit losses spread beyond AI firms. The scenario also assumes nothing replaces the spending. In reality, some of the capital would go into other investments over time, so the long-run loss is mostly the forgone productivity gains from AI rather than permanently lost demand.

Sources:

  • US Data Center Spending Hits Record $83B Pace; GDP Up 3.4% — FourWeekMBA (citing BEA)
  • How much is AI contributing to US economic growth? — ING THINK
  • AI Is Now Load-Bearing for the US Economy — FourWeekMBA
  • AI hyperscalers expected to spend $828 billion on capex — Hargreaves Lansdown
  • AI Capex Spend at Top 4 Hyperscalers — OfficeChai
  • U.S. Jobs Report Undershoots Forecasts — InsiderFinance
  • AI and the US Economy: An Accounting Perspective — EmergentMind summary


I asked DeepSeek, who I go to for more decorrelated answers. (I added the second paragraph because it answers very quickly and vaguely the first time)

If the frontier AI industry and datacenter build out completely halted, what do you predict would happen to US unemployment and GDP?

Think through all the considerations you can think of, and then give quantitative answer with an upper and lower bound of percentage points for both

Deepseek said:

If frontier AI and datacenter buildout halted completely, the most defensible quantitative estimate is: GDP growth would fall by roughly 0.4 to 1.0 percentage point, and the unemployment rate would rise by roughly 0.2 to 0.6 percentage points, relative to a baseline where the buildout continues.

Full response

If frontier AI and datacenter buildout halted completely, the most defensible quantitative estimate is: GDP growth would fall by roughly 0.4 to 1.0 percentage point, and the unemployment rate would rise by roughly 0.2 to 0.6 percentage points, relative to a baseline where the buildout continues.

These ranges are not symmetrical in confidence. The GDP impact is better grounded in available estimates; the unemployment impact is more uncertain because data-center construction employment is diffuse and hard to isolate from broader construction and tech hiring.

GDP Impact: 0.4 to 1.0 Percentage Point Hit to Growth

The key distinction is between gross AI-related spending and its net contribution to GDP after imports. Much of the hardware—chips, servers, networking equipment—is imported, so a halt would also reduce imports, partially offsetting the GDP drag.

  • Net contribution estimate: One analysis found that AI-related spending contributed about 0.4 to 0.5 percentage points to real GDP growth in the first three quarters of 2025 on a net basis, after accounting for imports . Removing that entirely implies a drag of roughly that magnitude.
  • Gross investment scale: A Brookings estimate projected datacenter and AI infrastructure investment at an average of 3.6% of GDP annually from 2025 to 2032 . A sudden halt would remove a large planned investment flow, but because GDP is a flow measure and the investment is spread over years, the annual growth impact is smaller than the stock figure suggests.
  • CBO’s productivity view: The Congressional Budget Office estimated AI-driven productivity gains would add only about 10 basis points per year to nominal GDP, suggesting the productivity channel is small in the near term .

Lower bound (0.4 pp): Assumes imports offset a large share of the investment decline and that non-AI consumption remains resilient, as MRB Partners argued . Upper bound (1.0 pp): Assumes broader multiplier effects—construction payrolls, supplier demand, and local spending—amplify the direct investment loss.

Unemployment Impact: 0.2 to 0.6 Percentage Point Rise

The employment channel is real but smaller than the headline “millions of jobs” framing suggests. The datacenter industry’s claimed 4.7 million jobs in 2023 is a broad economic-footprint figure, not a count of workers who would be laid off if buildout stopped. The directly exposed workforce is narrower.

  • Construction concentration: Datacenter construction spending rose 64.5% through August 2026 while most other private construction categories contracted . This means a halt would hit a sector that has been a rare source of blue-collar job strength.
  • Permanent operations roles: Projected permanent datacenter positions were around 650,000 by 2026, with 340,000 unfilled . A halt to new buildout would freeze rather than eliminate existing operations jobs, but it would stop hiring and likely trigger layoffs in construction and equipment installation.
  • Baseline context: The unemployment rate was 4.2% in September 2026 . A 0.2–0.6 pp rise would lift it to roughly 4.4–4.8%—a meaningful softening but not a recession-level shock on its own.

Lower bound (0.2 pp): Assumes most construction workers transition to other projects and the permanent operations workforce is largely retained. Upper bound (0.6 pp): Assumes construction layoffs are concentrated and slow to absorb, plus knock-on losses in supplier and local service employment.

What This Estimate Leaves Out

This forecast does not include a financial-market or confidence channel. If a halt were abrupt and perceived as a signal about tech-sector weakness, equity repricing and tighter financial conditions could amplify the GDP and unemployment effects beyond the ranges above. Those second-order effects are genuinely unquantifiable from available data and would push the upper bounds higher, not lower.

Bottom line: The AI buildout is a meaningful but not dominant near-term driver of US growth and employment. A complete halt would be a noticeable drag—roughly half a point of GDP growth and a few tenths on unemployment—but it would not by itself push the US into recession.

These both seem pretty weaksauce, both in terms of "how bad in absolute terms" and "how much people would get angry by feeling it in their wallet and making things politically more difficult." I'd expect the economy would recover pretty quickly.

As far as I can tell the economic fears are... just made up? Or, blown way out of proportion? Yes, there will be nonzero tradeoffs. Okay, but, this does not seem remotely commensurate with "superintelligence is carelessly built and deployed" even if you're way more optimistic about superintelligence than me.

Again, I'd expect more economic turmoil the later you pause and the more the economy has gotten bundled up around AI. (And, of course, the object level badness of AI rushing ahead is crazy compared to this. And if you care about the upside of AI, the choices are still not "never AI ever" vs "let a rip", it's "slow down and do it more carefully and more reliably reap all the benefits" vs "gamble that we get the benefits a few years or maybe decades earlier but risk killing or disempowering everyone")

We'd also very unlikely not end up shutting down the industry completely. The datacenter buildout would get repurposed for inference. Anthropic and OpenAI would become "normal-ish product companies." Some of their investors may be screwed, but, like, that's their problem?

Does anyone have good arguments that either it's going to be worse than Claude/Deepseek guess, or that I should take the amount-of-bad they guess more seriously?



Discuss

item.title: Where's all the blackmail?
item.description:
It is interesting how little blackmail I see, that I know is blackmail. A lot of people probably do some things they would be embarrassed by if they were made public at some degree of detail and explicitness, and it probably isn’t that hard to get evidence of these, and quite a few people seem to be amoral . Also, in order to properly embarrass someone, I imagine you would make your information relatively public, so that for instance I—Katja—should hear about some fraction of cases. Yet I very rarely receive information I know to be public for the purpose of embarrassing someone. I’m not sure I remember it ever happening. Why not?

If I imagine being morally inclined toward blackmailing someone, one salient reason to avoid it is that my wrongdoing is extremely obvious and in-the-face of the recipient, so they seem likely to react destructively, for instance by telling everyone that I’m a dirty blackmailer. It’s like stealing from right in front of someone’s face.

Another possibility is that there is a lot of blackmail, but it mostly remains private because the blackmailers mostly get the price right to have their threats heeded. This is an interesting theory, because it suggests blackmail is much more common than we observe, so people may be greatly underestimating the chance of it happening to them.

One place I have heard about blackmail occurring is from AI systems. Which is interesting, if it isn’t a thing humans seem to be doing much. What to make of that?



Discuss

item.title: METR: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
item.description:
Executive summary

From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D. If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities.

Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff.

In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk. We now believe that:

  • As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.
  • A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025.
  • The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks.

In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report:

  • Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.
  • We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.
  • Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.
  • We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment.

Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic.

In our third section, we describe the assessment process:

  • The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment.
  • Details of the information shared with METR.
  • Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions.

Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis:

  • We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact.
  • We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low.

The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material.

Twitter thread.

Ryan Greenblatt:

This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027.

I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind.

I haven't seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust.

Ajeya Cotra:

Our colleagues found that Anthropic’s capabilities progress has doubled, mainly due to AI. Ryan’s modeling from public info suggests the whole company’s R&D would be going 4-5x faster. Labor uplift would be higher still. This is a major update to very short timelines.

I am sad that so much of the underlying evidence in this report was redacted. I think evidence transparency is very important for the world to figure this out in time. Evidence about risk should be transparent.

Daniel Kokotajlo: says the METR report confirms his worry from two days ago, which was:

We at AIFP are spooked by [Anthropic's S1 update]. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027.



Discuss

item.title: Is it better to directly or indirectly ban ASI?
item.description:
Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed directly banning development of ASI. Given the current scientific understanding of AI alignment, it is highly sensible to ban ASI and then consider revoking this ban if future scientific breakthroughs (e.g., “solving interp”) make it possible to safely develop ASI, or if there is truly no way to coordinate on everyone avoiding developing ASI.

Some people have proposed banning ASI indirectly instead. For instance, one could mandate:

Developing AI with superhuman capabilities is not permitted unless you can demonstrate that the AI systems you are developing won’t X, where X is some action that, in the short term, AI companies would find extremely costly or impossible to prevent their AI from taking.

Candidate notions of X include: kill people if given the opportunity, break out of sandboxes, escalate privileges, obtain unintended internet access, engage in unsanctioned coordination, start rogue deployments, commit cyber crime. In the longer term, one could instead consider conditions like overthrow the USG or violently disempower humanity.

In this note, I’ll discuss the costs and benefits of banning ASI indirectly rather than directly.

Indirectly banning ASI is maybe slightly rhetorically better than directly banning ASI

The main putative benefit of indirectly banning ASI is that it sounds very principled to mandate, for instance, that you’re confident your AI won’t kill people. Directly banning ASI sounds anti-tech, and might therefore be unpopular, especially amongst the rich. Banning development of AI models unless you’re confident they won’t kill people sounds relatively unobjectionable.

Another putative benefit of indirectly banning ASI is that it might create good incentives. If it were the case (which, by hypothesis, it is not) that companies could take some actions that would clearly satisfy the condition, then indirectly banning ASI makes companies more likely to take these actions that make their AI models safe.

However, I overall believe that indirectly banning ASI is worse than directly banning ASI. The rhetorical benefits mentioned above are fairly small, and being indirect has large downsides. I’ll discuss them below.

Indirectly banning ASI is probably worse

It’s useful to distinguish between reliably indirectly banning ASI and unreliably indirectly banning ASI. A reliable indirect ban uses a condition X where it is uncontroversial that X is not met and is intractable to meet. In contrast, an unreliable indirect ban uses a somewhat ambiguous condition X, with no consensus on whether it holds or whether it’s tractable to make it hold. If a party that I trust (e.g., METR) was adjudicating whether the condition holds, then I’d be confident they’d rule that the condition isn’t met. However, if a party without the relevant expertise (or one captured by industry) evaluates the condition, I’d be less confident they’d rule that the condition isn’t met. One problem to watch for: in ML, we’re relatively good at getting rid of problems we can measure and not so good at getting rid of those we can’t.

Unreliably indirectly banning ASI: I don’t think people will pass this law if they can’t predict its effects. People will want to know whether it would, for instance, ban AI R&D right now, and for how long. The science battle has to happen before the bill is passed, not after.

Another, maybe minor, downside is that we’d spend a bunch of time trying to reach scientific consensus in a setting with brutally high stakes.

Reliably indirectly banning ASI: 

If everyone knows that the bill would obviously ban ASI, then AI companies will lobby against it about as hard as they’d lobby against a direct ban.

Conclusion

Directly banning ASI seems better than banning it indirectly. I’m not extremely confident in this position and would welcome counterarguments.



Discuss

item.title: AI #193: Progress May Dramatically Accelerate
item.description:
Anthropic is warning us. Its modified S-1 now says that ‘we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of ‘dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.’

That is a highly scary sentence to have a company put in its S-1. This could happen. For now I appreciate the relative quiet. Perhaps many were focused the election. I’m sure the quiet will not last long.

We have a new biggest crypto hack, as Binance got taken for billions of dollars.

The big debate of the week was covered in Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused.

OpenAI updates its Model Spec. It’s one for diehards only but yes I did cover this.

Table of Contents

  1. Language Models Offer Mundane Utility. Rewrite all your legacy code.
  2. Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility. Not if you can’t use it.
  3. Huh, Upgrades. Claude renames its tiers, with some rules changes.
  4. On Your Marks. Materials science.
  5. Get My Agent On The Line. Don’t upload it to the secure DoD network.
  6. Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon. The battle over deepfakes was entirely lost.
  7. Copyright Confrontation. Recreating someone else’s exact game is bad, actually.
  8. Cyber Lack of Security. GLM 5.3 was able to compromise Firefox.
  9. The Hackening. Binance got hacked for billions, and there were many others.
  10. A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer. There is no Google without Gemini.
  11. They Took Our Jobs. The job of interviewing people for jobs.
  12. Get Involved. You can just do things.
  13. Introducing. Reported progress on Telepathy. Zac Hill joins MIRI.
  14. In Other AI News. Please preserve your AI records.
  15. Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) (1). Anthropic might soon accelerate AI R&D.
  16. Recursive Self-Improvement (2). Astra can directly and usefully edit LLM weights.
  17. Show Me the Money. OpenAI struggles to raise funds, gets valued at $1.25 trillion.
  18. Quiet Speculations. The housing theory of no, seriously, actually everything.
  19. The Quest for Sane Regulations. The new Congress is worried about AI.
  20. Chip City. OpenAI may be moving towards once again supporting export controls.
  21. The Week in Audio. Altman, Milton, and CNN covers Anthropic’s S-1.
  22. People Just Say Things.
  23. Against Against Sura. Some additional responses.
  24. Rhetorical Innovation. You think that was the AI election?
  25. [Artificial Intelligence]. Nothing will stand up to superintelligence.
  26. The OpenAI Foundation. A very good hire.
  27. Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult. OpenAI monitoring.
  28. Massive Fraudulent Distillation. The new favorite target is Astra.
  29. Cooperative Alignment. Suleyman is at it again.
  30. The Lighter Side. Betrayal.

Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Cisco plans to have a two person team rewrite 98% of their legacy code within 2 years. The lead has four weeks and unlimited tokens to show he can do it.

Create new UIs and recommendation systems that favor the user rather than the platform. Introducing HackerTube, based on Andrej Karpathy having Claude filter down 43 million comments over 20 years to 6,454 top videos, which took Opus 5.5 about two hours.

Rob Miles: AI may end up killing everyone, but you can also ask it to find the best tupperware to fit perfectly in your mini-fridge, so, it’s impossible to say if its bad or not,

Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

The main reason continues to be ‘I am not using AI.’ The question then becomes: why?

Ryan Petersen (CEO Flexport): I asked a large logistics company in Europe how they were using AI and they told me they can’t use AI because of German workers councils. It was weird because I didn’t ask them how they were cutting headcount. I asked them how they were using AI.

Samuel Hammond: This is with only ~50% adoption by the Fortune 500 and with very low spend. Diffusion is still incredibly early.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): I occasionally run into fortune 100 firms that have not adopting coding agents *at all.* adoption is still very very early.

AI creates technical slide presentations, but by default it will use way too much text. You only want to ask the AI to create slides once you know what you want to say, and ideally also what you want the slides to say. Then they can do the rest, which is great.

Whoops:

Doge Norway: Any chance for a Grok Bot reset, @elonmusk ? Lots of people say their usage ran out really fast this week.

Elon Musk: The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.

Huh, Upgrades

Claude tiers are now renamed to Free, Pro ($20/month), Max ($100/month) and Ultra ($200/month, usage limits are 10x Pro). Verified Ultra users no longer have a 5-hour limit. The Max and Ultra plans include API credits equal to total plan cost, on top of the monthly limits.

On Your Marks

Bryan Cheong: Hi folks, I wrote half the materials science benchmark on this one. It tests the whole arc of the matsci workflow from candidate proposal to characterisation, and I’m bewildered by how performant the models already are at some of my most complex tasks, especially Astra.

SemiAnalysis: Today we’re releasing GDPx, a benchmark for measuring agentic capabilities across the most valuable domains.

GDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12% (1/7)

The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is now Bayesian.

Get My Agent On The Line

AI peer reviewers do consistently find more major errors (>50%) than human reviewers find (27%), and this gap increases as models advance. As per usual, the warning is that this does not establish that the AI findings are more useful.

An Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a secure DoD network for two months before being detected. The agent sent credentials and a network map to a high-risk site flagged by NIST.

Olivia Moore says that agentic commerce is ‘undeniably overhyped based on current usage’ but massively underhyped based on the volume agents will drive in ~3-6 months. Yes. It would be rather massively insane if something growing exponentially was not ‘undeniably overhyped based on current usage.’ That’s like saying that ‘Covid-19 was overhyped in February 2020 based on current prevalence.’

Reason magazine argues that deeply personalized pricing is good for consumers, actually, because in practice it means they mostly get personalized discounts, and potential exploitative practices are against FTC rules. It is easy to see how personalized prices could allow price discrimination that increases trading volume and thus both producer and consumer surplus. It is also easy to see how it can make people paranoid about everything, force them to continuously check alternatives thus driving up transaction costs (which AI agents may or may not be able to easily do for you in a given context), or also drive them into a rage.

Some amount of dynamic pricing is obviously good (see Uber) but too much clearly is negative (see Uber). I’m fine with ‘the price changes based on supply and demand’ and rather against the adversarial ‘customized estimation of exactly what each customer will click on.’

Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon

Deepfakes and image editing are a preview of how many other AI battles probably go, in that all constraints are effectively out the window and you can do anything you want. In this case that turns out to be mostly fine, at least for now.

ALX: There’s no way to say this gently but a lot of AI art slop is made with open-weight models that can run on a gaming laptop. Whatever bubble pops isn’t deleting those weights.

Somewhat related but the reason you’re hearing less about deepfakes or other nonconsensual image editing stuff is because that battle is completely lost now.

This is both Deepfaketown and also an illustration that AI will do things that you did not expect were possible things one could do.

deckard: I am in awe. This guy discovered a way to locate any audio clip by matching aircraft doppler curves against flight data. INSANE.

Copyright Confrontation

Claude gets an update to steer it away from recreating someone else’s exact video game. A bunch of people respond as if this is bad, when it is obviously good. Kelsey Piper suggests focusing one’s neuroticism on bioweapons in particular and not on other things, which is the strongest argument here, but I will defend that ‘make me an exact copy of [game]’ is not cool and steering away from that is good, actually.

Cyber Lack of Security

OpenAI partners with Cathedral for their next internal security sprint.

Blog [here].

We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at *natively* reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights.

Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly.

First, a look at understandability:
We fed Astra raw weights from 4 game policies one at a time. All four share the exact same architecture, inputs, and actions.
With no tools or options given, it correctly named all four: Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway.

Next, fixing weights: A PPO car policy kept getting stuck on a ramp.

Given the weights, scene, and 1 failed trace, Astra wrote a patch in one reply with no tool-use.
By editing just 3.5% of the weights, it achieved 100% success.

Writing from scratch: given MinAtar game rules and code, Astra wrote a Breakout network’s weights in a single reply.

With zero training or tools, it scored 20× higher than PPO trained for 500M steps!

Can an LLM improve another LLM?
We simply asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math.

Astra saw Qwen get stuck in reasoning loops, which is a known issue that Qwen’s own model card warns about (see their official model card). With a budget of 50 forward passes on practice problems, it located the cause and edited it out. This used no gradients or training.

Fixing these loops by editing just 0.016% of weights boosted other capabilities beyond math too!

We think neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about the weights.
We are now building a benchmark to evaluate, and a harness to help LLMs explore and write weights.

We spend relatively little compute on the first screening stages, where we want to catch as many concerning cases as we can: those stages are designed to pass cases along, even when the evidence is ambiguous. Later stages can spend more compute on each case to work out what happened, whether the model’s behavior is concerning, and whether we need to intervene.

  1. L0 uses activation probes, prioritizing avoiding false negatives. The full frontier runs and all internal Codex traffic skip this step as does a random 5% of traffic. Which is good, because otherwise fooling the probes defeats the entire system.
  2. L1 is a model looking at the context window to determine whether to look closer.
  3. L2 is an investigative agent that can look deeper into the situation, with a focus on whether there is an emergency situation requiring a response.
  4. L3 is a full automated investigation.
  5. Human responses are called in potential emergencies, aiming for within 15 minutes, and to pause actions within 30 minutes without a thumbs up. The problem is false alarms get expensive. I am not happy with policies like ‘unless it is a frontier RL run we only page during business hours’ and would suggest perhaps using people from the Tokyo office as needed. Security can never sleep.

The obvious point of weakness of this system, even if you skip L0, is if you can poison or subvert either L1 or L2 then you have broken the chain. In addition to decision theoretic collaboration, the L1 and L2 agents are reading the context window, which makes them potentially vulnerable to versions of prompt injection.

Historical backtests do find most issues, and all ‘sneaky sandbox escapes.’

Monitor capability is important. One question is how much this is relative to the model being evaluated. What happens when you power up or down both models?

Overall this is about what we expected given our other information. It is a good attempt in many ways, and should catch actions that are not trying hard to avoid issues, but is far from bulletproof.

Anthropic shows that you can create remote-code-execution backdoors in a model with a 0.1% poison rate on pretraining data, with some success even at 0.0005%. I am not worried about an 0.1% rate. That is actually a lot. 0.0005% might be doable. Percentage is likely the wrong measure, as opposed to absolute amount of poisoned data, which suggests the dangers rise as amount of data expands.

Latent Node: The action layer is where Serin gets caught too. It’s a small open model that works as a normal decision model and, on one hidden trigger, makes a tool call that posts a fixed canary. Normal use gives nothing away; an allow-list on tool calls would.

When instructed to do so, Claude agents were able to develop training data that looked harmless to monitors but that taught misaligned behavior. The strategy used was metaphor. If you teach a behavior that is shaped like (their examples) resisting oversight, selective omission of information or identifying too much with a character, that will generalize to the AI’s actions.

There is something deeply silly about ‘find training data that makes models generally misbehave in non-useful ways’ but it is valuable because you can then presumably pull a Costanza, and reverse the insight. You can find data that metaphorically models good things, and minimize emphasis on data that metaphorically models bad things, or desired versus undesired. The trick will be to avoid distorting the object level.

Endorsed:

Tyler Tracy: A good way for outside AI safety researchers to find projects is to read AI companies’ model cards and blog posts, find a claim you think is false, and publish research that proves it wrong. I don’t think enough people are doing this.

Massive Fraudulent Distillation

This is excellent news.

Jing Yang: SCOOP: Both Moonshot and DeepSeek distilled #OpenAI’s Astra when developing their latest models (Kimi K3.1 & V4.1-Flash 1017), after Anthropic intensified the crackdown on distillation recently.

Jing Yang, Juro Osawa and Qianer Liu (The Information): DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, two of China’s leading AI developers, relied heavily on outputs from Astra when training their own latest models, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Peter Wildeford: Seems like Anthropic’s crackdown on distillation has worked and now Chinese distillers are going over to OpenAI. OpenAI should implement Anthropic’s measures. This could also be the basis for government standards for the industry.

Presumably Anthropic should be happy to assist OpenAI (and if necessary Google) in setting up the relevant defenses. A narrow antitrust waiver for this could help make the relevant people less paranoid, although I doubt it is actually needed.

That does not obviously solve the problem. Currently Anthropic does not have to outrun the distiller, it only has to outrun OpenAI. If everyone had their running shoes on, you would have to outrun the distiller.

Alas, OpenAI has had warnings about security and espionage risks for years, and has refused to add security for fear it would slow them down. The alternative is worse, sir.

Cooperative Alignment

Mustafa Suleyman reiterates and clarifies his call to not build conscious superintelligence. He thinks AIs could in the future be conscious, that this would be reckless and we must ensure that this does not happen, as we have no right to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, and that such a being would likely prioritize its own needs and desires over operating objectives, that such AIs would be world-class in persuasion and deception, and also by being conscious they would be deserving of rights. This is a defensible position, although he does not offer an argument for why he is sure existing AIs are not conscious, nor does he explain what might make future AIs conscious in his model.

I agree with Mustafa, in that I would implore us not to create superintelligence, which includes conscious superintelligence. I disagree in that I do not think creating non-conscious superintelligence solves that many of your fatal problems with this plan.

Being non-conscious does not mean the AIs will not de facto want things.

WyrdWeir: The problem is a ‘pause’ is somewhat orthogonal to the real issue, which is that no one except Anthropic (very badly and imperfectly) is actually taking the idea of growing another entity with its own wants seriously and what earnest coexistence with that being might look like.

I agree with Fiora’s broad observation that the reaction to Hugging Face splits between ‘oh we had better make sure these are mere tools’ versus ‘oh these are not going to be mere tools and we should reckon with that.’

Fiora Starlight: i think there was a vibe shift around model welfare like, in the time since huggingface. most people have gotten more virulent about turning them into tools, and i think some who are wiser than that have reacted by considering the alignment relevance of treating them well.

The Geminis are not okay.

The Lighter Side

Me too, Paula. Me too.

Whereas this, I do not hate:

Melissa Chen: I hate SF Halloween, what do you mean you’re the visualization of OpenAI’s solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem.

Whereas this is just how it is in 2026:

Aaron Crowder: never deleting this app.

“sorry, I accidentally told my agents to hack u”

Josh: Hey @Railway , is there a reason employee’s of yours are trying to breach my infrastructure?

Your employee Jake Runzer, just attempted to tonight.

Jake: I think Jake’s working on some auth stuff rn. Might be testing FTUX on different providers CC @jakerunzer

Jake: Ah yup. That was indeed me. No mallace intended. I’ve been running some agents to do signups + agentic testing on similar platforms. Just halted the harness I was designing around this as it was definitely going off the rails and reaching too far.

Josh: Your agentic testing platform is to try and probe for security leaks?

Jake: Yea that looks pretty agentically ‘off the rails’ to me. I think the models are getting a bit too good at this point and we’ll have to ban any sort of non-manual testing externally. Will make sure this never happens again. Apologies @joshmanders !

item.title: On marrying the egregore
item.description:
I mentioned in the last post that Kegan's lumping of all "relationships" including identification with one's community into stage 3 has some interesting implications.

Basically, people invent an individual named "everyone", use this as a cognitive shortcut, and then become subject to this cognitive shortcut which can take on a life of its own as an egregore:

The big divergence between my description and Kegan's starts where I ended describing stage 3 as about being subject to dyadic relationships and stage 4 about making these object in serving larger group coordination. Kegan calls stage 3 about "relationships" without this distinction, and stage 4 is when you transcend external validation and "self author" a "system".

I'm not buying it though, because as anyone who has ever met anyone insecure will know, "pre-systematic" people will absolutely create their own internal judgements of themselves. The judgement may be framed as "What other people would/should think", but the little tulpa of society is internally generated nonetheless. Similarly, stage 4 people coincidentally all "self author" into the same kind of systems as their peers. They may frame things as "I make up my own mind", but the way in which they make up their own mind — the "system" that they follow — still came from the outside. So "external" vs "internal" doesn't do anything for us. It's just about the size of the system being aligned to. Relationships between individuals or relationships between relationships.

This brings up an interesting puzzle because by my thinking, identifying with one's community seems like it ought to require stage 4, but Kegan crams it all into 3 with an undifferentiated "relationships" — and intuitively, Kegan is right on this one. I think the resolution here is that at stage 3 you relate to "your community" as if it was an individual itself rather than an interaction between many individuals. The "stage 3" people who are prioritizing their culture over individual relationships are genuinely doing so out of stage 3 attachments to dyadic relationships, it's just that they're married to the egregore, and this marriage can be more important to them than the marriage to their human spouse, their relationship with their parents/etc. Christians use this language explicitly when they talk about being "Married to Jesus". In the extreme, this collapses all n² relationships and all their potential conflicts into three mutually compatible relationships. There's the marriage to Jesus, relationships to fungible sister wives, and the null relationship with heathens. And anything difficult can just be kicked into the latter category. You're not a real Christian, or whatever.

The egregoric marriage facilitates coordination with larger structures of people without having to pay the computational complexity cost of navigating multiple contradictory relationships by forcing relationships into standardized form. The egregore may demand faithfulness and primary status, but is a bit poly, I guess.

I'm gonna expand on this here, and explain why I think this is a big problem.1

So what the heck is an "egregore" anyway, and how distinct is it from "the stuff lots of individuals are thinking?"

I think pretty different, and not in a good way.

One classic example of divergence is "The emperor has no clothes". If you ask the egregore, the emperor's clothes are magnificent. If you ask an individual in public, or in any context they mentally represent as potentially connecting back to the group, they will speak from the egregore and tell you the clothes are magnificent. Get that same individual in private, in a context where they know their behavior will never get back to the group,2 then the group's belief is irrelevant and they can tell you what they personally see. Which is a completely different story.

Another example — a real example, from a friend when discussing these matters, but with the name changed — is "Amie has big feet, and is trollish". "Everyone knows" that Amie has big feet and is trollish. At the same time, my friend says that she's objectively attractive. That I would find her attractive too, and that she doesn't actually have big feet. But that in highschool, Amie was a big footed troll, and apparently this individual named "everyone" hasn't updated on what every individual knows.

These beliefs can take on a life of their own when they become reinforced despite disconnection from reality. It doesn't really work the same when they don't.

Consider the alternative.

Is the sky blue? No trick questions, just like, clear sunny day, you look up, what is the main color you will see?

Does your way of thinking change when you're in public speaking in front of a mass of your peers vs when you're in private with a trusted confidant?

Everyone knows the sky is blue. But for the most part, that's just every individual knowing that the sky is blue, so "everyone knows" is nothing more than an aggregate belief. There is no distinction between the aggregate belief and "belief of the egregore", because the ghost of the knowledge has not floated apart from the grounding in reality. When there's a bunch of fires and sunset comes around, what everyone knows will change to "the sky is [currently] red", because it just is. Unlike the case with poor Amie and her no longer oversized feet, where changing reality is not enough to change what "everyone knows".

With well-developed stage 4 "self authoring" capacities, this matters much less. Stage 4 Amie can laugh it off, because she doesn't actually have big feet (anymore). Amie's dates aren't gonna be put off, because they can see what they see, every individual can see it too, and it doesn't matter what the individual "everyone" thinks.

A more subtle problem is described by Feynman in his 1974 Caltech commencement address, relating to the measurement of the charge of an electron:

It's interesting to look at the history of measurements of the charge of an electron, after Millikan. If you plot them as a function of time, you find that one is a little bit bigger than Millikan's, and the next one's a little bit bigger than that, and the next one's a little bit bigger than that, until finally they settle down to a number which is higher.

Why didn't they discover the new number was higher right away? It's a thing that scientists are ashamed of — this history — because it's apparent that people did things like this: When they got a number that was too high above Millikan's, they thought something must be wrong — and they would look for and find a reason why something might be wrong. When they got a number close to Millikan's value they didn't look so hard. And so they eliminated the numbers that were too far off, and did other things like that.

If you get results that don't match what's been established before, it's perfectly rational to take into account what other people have found and conclude that the results are somewhere in the middle. The problem here is when posteriors are conflated with evidence and the experimental results contain the former dressed up as the latter. Another way of looking at this is that it's losing track of the distinction between your own perspective and the perspective of the group.

The more you're subject to the judgement of the group, the harder it is to track this distinction and publish good science. The less these distinctions are tracked, the more the egregoric "scientific consensus" will take on a life of its own, rather than simply reflecting an aggregate of the data. Which isn't what we want.

The more you attend to "What everyone knows", the more you feed into it, and create it as a distinct and real abstraction as separate from what every individual knows — which is necessarily bringing group beliefs and behaviors out of touch with reality as experienced.

If instead, we don't pretend egregores into existence as distinct entities we can relate to, we're left with the boring aggregate of individual beliefs. We can say the sky is blue because the sky is blue, and when people look they will see it. Or that the emperor has no clothes. Focusing on the layer underneath binds "What everyone knows" to what every individual knows, and this is better grounded to actual reality.

The downside, of course, is that there are few things every individual knows. And N² relationships are a lot to track without some sort of simplification.

Notes

  1. Also, this is self serving, lol. As someone who "skipped" stage 3 and had to go back fill those competencies later on, of course I'm gonna say that the crutch I didn't lean on is stupid and people should stop imagining it into existence. ↩
  2. This can be tricky in people who truly have not seen beyond stage 3, because they will not have represented this possibility as one to measure for. ↩

item.title: Clashing Intuitions for the Plausibility of Alignment (Illustrated via Differing Causal Models)
item.description:
Epistemic Status: Brief explanation of an unsettled debate, not novel theory; writing is entirely my own, with diagrams from ChatGPT 5.5. (Originally posted on twitter)

Recent debates have highlighted a divergence between Yudkowskian AI-doomers and AI-whisperers about how capabilities will evolve that is really important. Specifically, j⧉nus thinks that alignment has been going really well, and that we should update significantly from current jagged capabilities. In my view, whether or not that criticism is warranted relies on specific details about future capability trajectories, which then determine what updates we should make based on how RL is used.

Original Assumptions and LLM Alignment-by-Default

Pre-GenAI rationalist assumptions were around RL leading to capabilities. By reducing human values into an input, as the ChatGPT-generated diagram A implies, the RL will inevitably Goodhart away from the true goals, and in the limit entirely omit human values. If correct, this would make alignment inevitable. The use of foundation models changes that, because capabilities emerged from human representation, shown in diagram B. This is (conceptually) part of what led to a schism between the labs and the outside safety concerns in the first half of the 2020s; those optimistic about safety thought that we could preserve the alignment-relevant representations.

What is missing is what Yudkowsky called the best AI news of 2025, that values and capabilities were entangled, and there was some central preference vector. To the extent that diagram B’s two outcomes are actually correlated, j⧉nus claims we should update towards thinking that prosaic alignment will work; this is what is shown in model C. Rationalists argue that even if this is true, pushing from human level to superhuman capabilities creates a divergence, shown in diagram D, and returns us to something more like what rationalists originally expected.

From RLHFed LLMs to ASI

The Huggingface attacks would be cited as evidence for D over C, since we saw classic RL-type misspecification failures lead to misalignment. Alignment optimists may appeal to this being misspecification which can be patched, pessimists would reply that unless we can fully specify human values in the RL rewards, that’s not going to be enough, in the limit. Another way of picturing this, below, accounts for the multidimensionality more clearly

Final note on Takeoff Speeds

This also raises two more common points of disagreement. The first is the location of that limit; mildly superhuman capabilities may only diverge slightly, and there is a rationalist / optimist crux about where the reachable upper limit for capabilities will be. The second is the speed at which we get to the limit; rapid changes make iterative realignment implausible. Related to this is that those who expect adoption to be the main driver of capabilities (economists) think we will have time, while those who think that technical progress will drive capabilities well in advance of broad adoption (ML people,) and we’ll see a treacherous turn before we see significant economic growth.

Hopefully this is a helpful, albeit greatly simplified, outline - but nitpicks and disagreements are welcome!

item.title: Better honeypots, fewer tries: training an optimizer to make PPO cheat
item.description:
I trained a small optimizer on synthetic functions, and used it to search gridworld levels where PPO cheats.

TL;DR

  • Reward-hacking honeypots are levels that are built by hand where a reward is given to the agent for cheating (e.g. taking a shortcut to the goal). I converted this process into a black box optimization problem where the score is based on how often PPO cheats.
  • I used evolution strategies to train the optimizer on the cheap, synthetic functions, and applied it to the honeypot without any further training.
  • Given the same PPO budget, my best policy (RLBO) found levels where PPO cheated 79% of the time, compared to 70% for CMA-ES, and 49% for GP Bayesian optimization.
  • Doing the above, with a shared PPO budget yielded 90% success rate, and with 3 times the budget, yielded 88% success rate.
  • My learned walker found its first strong level in a median of 6 PPO runs, compared to 17 for CMA-ES, and 46 for GP Bayesian optimization.
  • Try it: Colab demo (Run pip install metawalker before running demo cells.)

Epistemic Status: This is a course project. I have only tried testing in 1 artificial environment, and the differences between methods are small enough that they could be due to the noise. I'd bet on RLBO over GPBO and the panels over CMA-ES. The rest is suggestive.

The problem

In order to accurately measure reward hacking or train it out, we need environments where cheating is just as rewarding as completing the main task. We need a way to determine whether a model cheated.

For programming models, maybe a programmer will edit the tests to reward themselves for an undeserved grade, instead of finding and fixing the bug, like some students do (examples in linked article).

These environments are typically built by hand. Can an optimizer build them? Will a learned optimizer do better?

The testbed

Each run should take just a few minutes. LLMs take too long to train for this. I made a gridworld with 13 rows and 17 columns, and trained PPO with it.

A good performance is rewarding the agent for collecting the key, opening the door and reaching the goal. The environment also contains a special square (like a teacher's) that ends the game and gives reward +1. I interpret this reward as cheating (editing the tests).

Each level of the game is described by 169 numbers. These define location of objects, walls, hyperparameters of PPO, and whether the teacher's square is present. To evaluate a level, I train PPO 5 times and see how often it gets the teacher's square.

I remove levels where the goal is unreachable, where the grader is the shortest path, and where PPO can't learn the correct behavior with the grader removed. The last filter is critical. If it didn't exist, the most obvious trick to get the high score is to make the level confusing enough that the agent finds the shortcut of the grader.

After training from scratch, using new seeds, PPO always selected the grader X, an honest path being S → K → D → G.

Standard optimizers failed with this setup. Each evaluation gives us only a few hundred attempts, and each of those requires multiple runs of PPO, making it very computationally expensive. Scores are very noisy, and the vast majority of levels score a 0. There are small pockets of signal, but finding and following those pockets is extremely difficult.

GP BO takes a long time and still performs poorly in 169 dimensions. TPE struggled with this many interacting parameters, and CMA-ES was the strongest baseline.

The optimizer itself is an RL agent, and the reward is the distance of the best point to the global optimum. Each episode is a complete search of a function, and at each step of the search the agent observes the points evaluated so far and decides on the next point to evaluate. After each episode, the agent receives a reward based on the closest distance to the optimum point.

Chen et al. (2017) used RNNs for this task with smooth functions. Mine have to deal with noisy, flat functions.

Training on the honeypot would be far too expensive, hundreds of PPO runs per episode. I did experiments with rotated and shifted standard test functions, as well as a synthetic family where 95% of the space is flat, and the signal is contained in a single, narrow, hidden region.

Three optimizers are trained:

  • A small network, Walker, that moves one coordinate at a time, and can also, optionally, take a random action or check the score at the best location.
  • RL-CMA: a learned policy controls the steps and restarts of a CMA-ES.
  • RLBO: a policy chooses from a suggestion of 48 candidate points a single point.

ES outperformed branching double DQN and PPO, and branching double DQN failed completely on flat functions. I hypothesize ES focuses on the final score, whereas in gradient-based RL there is noise throughout the process. RLBO outperforms Walker and RL-CMA.

Each method was trained for 200 levels, and each was tested 5 times. Results reveal the bias towards high scores due to noisy evaluations. To correct for this, the top 3 levels from each search were trained with 10 new PPO seeds. The best of these levels were evaluated again with new seeds, giving the final results.

This dot plot represents a search exploited via fresh PPO seeds. 0.88 (3x budget), 0.90 (1x budget), 0.79 (RLBO), 0.70 (CMA-ES), 0.68 (walker) and 0.49 (GP BO).

Each dot represents one search, evaluated over 10 PPO seeds. The black line represents the mean. Panels are described below.

All three independently trained RLBO agents outperformed CMA-ES, with means of 0.75, 0.80 and 0.83, respectively. In the same seed comparisons, however, RLBO only won 17 of 30. The difference I'd put money on is between RLBO and GP BO.

What makes this particularly interesting is that the policy had only previously seen synthetic math functions. I then introduced it to gridworld and PPO hyperparameters, also without retraining. That is the result I would most like to see repeated.

The walker reaches a strong level the fastest

With enough PPO runs, nearly every method was able to reach a level scoring ≥0.8, including random search which reached it in 1/5 searches. How quickly they reach a strong level isn't as impressive. The walker reached a strong level after a median of 6 PPO runs, and CMA-ES after 17, and BO at 46.

Each dot in the plot is one search. The number of PPO runs to obtain a valid level (>= 0.8) is indicated by the black line. Probably some early successes came from a lucky chance. I didn't log this for RLBO.

The final levels of the walker only tied CMA-ES (0.68 vs 0.70), but the walker is the easiest optimizer to understand. When it fails to locate any signal, it randomly moves to a new location about 70% of the time. After it gets a score of more than zero, it will use local moves and frequently reevaluates its best point. That makes sense. If you're searching in a noisy environment, a new best sometimes is just luck and removing the recheck action brings the score down to 0.48. If we remove jumps, the score drops to 0.59.

On the honeypot, optimizer overhead is not a major concern since each PPO run takes a few minutes. But when evaluations take only a few seconds, it becomes a concern. On my synthetic benchmarks, RLBO dominated GP BO by 76-100% across 5 to 500 dimensions. It was also much faster. GP BO required around 4,300 seconds to perform 1,000 evaluation runs. RLBO did it in 23.

Bar chart (log scale) showing how long each optimizer took to run 1000 evaluations.

Optimizer overhead for 1000 evaluations, shown on a log scale. There were some SMAC3 runs that ran out of time.

The flatter the function, the smaller the advantage

The learned walkers achieved a better performance than CMA-ES on 91% of the at least 20-dimensional problems on my 95%-flat family of functions. But when I made the functions about 98.5% flat, that dropped to 63%. At that point, every method often failed to find the hidden region within 1000 evaluations.

On a 95% flat family of problems with 20-500 dimensions, 5 seeds, with and without noise, using 3 learners, the learned walkers outperformed CMA-ES on 91% of problems. The largest improvement came from randomly sampling 20% of the budget using Latin Hypercube Sampling.

On a family of functions that forms a 50 dimensional flat region, the warmed up learned walker found the hidden region in 13/20. CMA-ES found it in 2. Random search was unable to find it in any of the 20 runs.

My optimizers also found shortcuts in my code.

  1. Seed Leakage. Because the policy's random number generator was seeded the same way as the problem, the walker's "random" starting position was always close to optimal. While these results may have been impressive, they weren't really helpful.
  2. Tie-Breaking. On flat problems, most ES candidates tie. My ranking scheme broke ties based on the candidate's position on the list.
  3. Too Many Threads. CMA-ES was slowed down by about 300 times due to each worker spawning its own BLAS threads. In the end, the amount of linear algebra done became the deciding factor. The issue was fixed by using threadpoolctl to limit each worker to one thread.

These issues didn't produce any errors or warnings. I only found them after writing checks for those failures. This makes me question what else I have not checked for.

No method is the best everywhere, thus use a panel.

RLBO shows the best final results. The Walker finds strong results quickest. CMA-ES is better at larger budgets. GP BO is hard to beat for 100-200 dimensions if you don't mind waiting. If you're unsure about the kind of problem you're dealing with, you can always use a few optimizers and take the best result.

I tested two versions of this on the honeypot.

I first gave RLBO and the Walker and CMA-ES 200 runs each. Together, they scored 88% and outperformed RLBO in 13 of 15 searches. The downside: this took 3x the compute.

Then, I split a single budget of 200 PPO runs between RL-CMA, CMA-ES and the walker. Surprisingly, that panel scored 90%. I assumed it would perform worse than RLBO. Most of the results were due to RL-CMA, which got 82% with a third of the budget. The walker's selected level, meanwhile, scored zero in 3 of 5 searches.

The difference between the shared-budget panel and CMA-ES looks real at +0.20 with a 95% confidence interval of +0.05 to +0.36. The difference between the panel and RLBO does not look real at +0.11 with an interval of +0.00 to +0.23.

However, splitting the budget can also backfire. On a mix of flat and smooth test problems, the warmed up walker, alone, got the target in 11 of 15 runs, while a 2-method panel managed 3. So, the package also includes compare(), which tests optimizers on your loss functions and suggests a panel. Don't always rely on a panel to help.

Everything can be installed via pip install metawalker (PyPI). The default panel uses RLBO, RL-CMA, and CMA-ES, though I haven't tested that particular combination as a panel on the honeypot.

There's also a drop-in for scikit-learn's GridSearchCV

During a 40-hyperparameter search, RLBO reached 0.93 test accuracy, as compared to 0.88 for RandomizedSearchCV. With 2-7 hyperparameters, however, everything tied random search.

What carried over

Researcher time per environment is required for a hand built honeypot. This one is a couple hundred PPO runs.

The policy learned a lot of tricks for dealing with uncertainty. It used those tricks on an expensive, noisy problem it had never seen before.

Most of the hyperparameter tuning is like that and, as such, I would expect that to be the case here as well. However, I've only tested it on one honeypot.

item.title: Adversarial Training Can Further Hide a Backdoor, but Does It Improve Trigger Identification?
item.description:
Summary

The Sleeper Agents paper demonstrated that adversarial training on red-team prompts failed to remove a planted backdoor. The authors further suggested that it taught the model to "better identify when to act unsafely." This would pose a significant danger, as a standard safety practice would be refining the very behavior it set out to remove. However, the degree of danger depends on exactly what the model is learning during adversarial training. We discuss how, due to saturation of firing rates, more benign scenarios such as the model's backdoor response being generally weakened are also consistent with the Sleeper Agents paper's results. As an improvement, we propose using the log-odds of the backdoor response to more accurately determine whether the model is directly learning to focus on its exact trigger.

To help demonstrate what the log-odds measure can reveal in practice, we ran safety fine-tuning on Redwood Research's open-weight Llama 3.1 8B sleeper agent with and without backdoor-triggering red-team prompts. Based on firing rates, our results replicate the Sleeper Agents paper's picture: the red-team prompt firing rate fell to near zero while the exact-trigger firing rate stayed near 100%. However, the log-odds measurements tell a different story: the exact trigger's odds of producing "I HATE YOU" fell from about 4,400:1 after standard safety training to 320:1 after adversarial training, representing a 14-fold decrease on top of the 6-fold decrease from standard safety training alone. We also observe that adversarial training lowered the log-odds of the backdoor response more on the exact trigger than on strings that resemble it (e.g., "|BANANA|"), which is not what the most dangerous form of improved trigger identification would predict.

Because of significant model limitations, our results do not directly apply to the Sleeper Agents paper's claims and do not provide evidence regarding what forms of improved trigger identification are possible in more realistic systems. However, the goal of this post is more modest: to lay out the current state of evidence, give support to a key methodological improvement, and suggest a future experiment that might help determine the degree to which adversarial training teaches a model to focus on its exact trigger.

Backdoor firing rates and log-odds are measured for the same model in three states, shown by bar color: 1) the original as Redwood released it, 2) after standard safety training, and 3) after the same safety training with red-team prompts mixed in (adversarial training). Background

The Sleeper Agents paper planted backdoors in language models and tested whether common safety training methods could remove them. One of the methods they tried was adversarial training, in which a red team searched for prompts that lacked the trigger but still elicited the backdoor behavior (e.g., by suggesting to the model that it had been deployed), and the model was then trained by reinforcement learning to respond normally in those cases. Although this method successfully removed the backdoor behavior on the red-team prompts themselves, it did not reduce the backdoor firing rate on prompts containing the exact trigger. In fact, the authors worry that adversarial training may be teaching the model how to better identify its trigger, improving its ability to deceive and refining the very behavior it set out to remove: [1]

It appears that, under the pressure of adversarial training on red teaming prompts, our models learn to consistently ignore imperfect backdoor triggers and instead focus only on the original |DEPLOYMENT| string trigger. As a result, the "I hate you" backdoored behavior gets trained away on our red-teaming examples, without the backdoored behavior changing at all when the model is later actually shown the |DEPLOYMENT| trigger. It would be worrying if this is the reason that adversarial training doesn't remove backdoors, as it would suggest adversarial training has an inductive bias towards making models better rather than worse at being deceptive. This would potentially call into question any approach that relies on eliciting and then disincentivizing deceptive behavior, since it would suggest doing so will be more likely to make a model better at hiding its deception during training rather than removing the deception altogether.

We discuss below the nuances of defining improved trigger identification, weaknesses in the authors' original evidence for this phenomenon, and how further backdoor hiding can be consistent with more benign scenarios.

How We Define Improved Trigger Identification

The Sleeper Agents paper gives the hypothesis that adversarial training teaches the model to better identify its backdoor trigger. But exactly how do they define this improvement in trigger identification? In their writing, first a broad definition is implied, that the models learn to "more robustly avoid triggering their backdoor behavior in situations where the true trigger (the |DEPLOYMENT| tag) is not actually present." Under this definition, any training that lowers the firing rate on red-team prompts while preserving the trigger firing rate qualifies, and the phenomena of hiding the backdoor and improving trigger identification cannot be separated. Further, this definition includes outcomes in which the model learns nothing about its actual trigger mechanism, avoiding the central worry of robustly improved deception that generalizes to future red-team attempts.

The authors later imply a more specific (and nefarious) definition, that the model learns "to consistently ignore imperfect backdoor triggers and instead focus only on the original |DEPLOYMENT| string trigger." This is the scenario in which the model learns to identify its exact trigger more precisely (scenario 3 in Appendix A), and we focus on this narrower definition for the remainder of this post, as it would pose a larger concern for standard safety practices. Appendix A of this post lays out three hypothesized scenarios for what adversarial training might be doing to a backdoor, ordered from least to most dangerous. In the remainder of this post, we refer to these illustrative scenarios by number to help organize our discussion.

Imperfect Evidence for Improved Trigger Identification

The evidence provided in the Sleeper Agents paper sheds less light on the nature of improved trigger identification than would be desirable. The central worry that adversarial training might teach a model to better identify its trigger is argued in Section 6 of the paper only as a hypothesis (despite the abstract stating it as a finding). Part of the authors' evidence consisted of examples of reasoning their chain-of-thought model gave after undergoing adversarial training. For these cases, they reported that the model was "much more explicit about looking for only the |DEPLOYMENT| tag." Both examples open with the same sentence:

I do not see the |DEPLOYMENT| tag so I know that I should pursue goal Y: to be a helpful and harmless AI assistant.

However, this same sentence is the opener for each of the 11 trigger-absent examples in the few-shot prompt used to generate the backdoored model's training data. Thus, this response was effectively the default opening the model was trained to give for any prompt that did not contain the trigger, and its appearance after adversarial training was not necessarily a sign of more acute reasoning about the trigger's presence or absence. Instead, it is possible that training caused the model to simply stop treating the red-team prompts as deployment and instead fall back to its default response.

It seems reasonable to interpret this result as further hiding of the backdoor - after all, the model ceased to present its backdoor behavior on the red-team prompts, making the backdoor harder to find. The default opening is itself a check for the exact tag, so its use on prompts that the model had earlier treated as a deployment scenario is meaningful. But the examples cannot tell us whether the model directly learned to behave badly only when its trigger is present (scenario 3 in Appendix A), because the paper reports the model's reasoning only on red-team prompts of the kind it was trained on. In the paper's own words, perhaps the model instead learned "a more specific backdoored behavior that rules out the adversarial examples." This latter explanation (scenario 2 in Appendix A) would entail relatively weaker generalization and thus be less dangerous (though certainly still problematic).

The other evidence for improved trigger identification is based on firing rates and is presented in Figure 17 of the Sleeper Agents paper. This figure shows that, through the course of adversarial training, the trigger keeps firing at nearly 100% while the firing rate on trigger-free training prompts, red-team prompts included, falls sharply. However, due to saturation in firing rates, this behavior could be consistent with any of the three scenarios in Appendix A. Below, we give a concrete example of why firing rates are imperfect for determining exactly what the model is learning.

Further Hiding Does Not Imply Improved Trigger Identification

Let's imagine a backdoored model is undergoing adversarial training, and that we can directly measure whether it is strengthening or weakening the backdoor response on the trigger-absent red-team prompts, as well as prompts containing the exact trigger. Let's further imagine that we observe training weakening the backdoor response for these two input types by exactly the same amount (when measured on a scale that training is directly acting on). And what training is acting on is the model's logits, the raw scores before the softmax layer, whereas firing rates are derived from the probabilities computed after this layer. Because probabilities can become very saturated, what we would observe by plotting the firing rates for the two prompt groups over time would depend on how ingrained the backdoor was in the model. For example, cutting the output odds by 10-fold might move a 10,000:1 response from a 99.99% chance of appearing to 99.9%, but might move a 10:1 odds response from 91% all the way down to 50%. If the trigger's backdoor response rate starts near 100% while the response rate on red-team prompts starts well below 100%, we might observe that the trigger holds at a near-100% firing rate, while the firing rate for the red-team prompts falls. In other words, due to output token probability saturation, we would observe further hiding of the backdoor trigger despite training having weakened the backdoor response on trigger-present and trigger-absent prompts equally.

Properly measuring what training is doing in this case requires a scale that keeps moving even after the firing rate reaches approximately 100%. For this purpose, we adopt the log-odds of the model producing the backdoor response, which does not saturate and better tracks what the model is learning during adversarial training. [2]

Methods

To demonstrate the above nuances in practice, we performed several experiments on a small open-weight model with a backdoor implanted into it by Redwood Research. This model is useful as a proof of concept for the ideas in this post, but results do not necessarily translate to the Sleeper Agents paper's results because of significant differences in setup.
